fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Deterministic regular expressions are a grammar formalism for defining regular expressions that correspond to deterministic regular languages.
In the spirit of Bruggemann-Klein and Wood and Krishaswami and Yallop, inductively define the deterministic regular expressions in terms of their nullability, first set, and followlast set:
\epsilon , the grammar accepting only the empty string.
\texttt {"}c\texttt {"}, the grammar only accepting the length 1 string comprising the character c for some character c drawn from the alphabet
r \otimes r', the concatenation of r and r' where \neg \mathsf {Null}(r) and \mathsf {FLast}(r) \cap \mathsf {First}(r') = \emptyset
r \oplus r', the disjunction of r and r' where \neg (\mathsf {Null}(r) \land \mathsf {Null}(r')) and \mathsf {First}(r) \cap \mathsf {First}(r') = \emptyset
{r}^{*}, the Kleene star of r where \neg \mathsf {Null}(r) and \mathsf {FLast}(r) \cap \mathsf {First}(r) = \emptyset

In each of the above constructors, the constraints on \mathsf {First}(r) and \mathsf {FLast}(r) remove sources of ambiguity in a regular expressions. They provide a sound guarantee that the resulting regular expression has at most one parse for any string.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Deterministic regular languages
fr:frontmatter.fr:meta: @InProceedings{10.1007/3-540-55210-3_182, author="Br{\"u}ggemann-Klein, Anne and Wood, Derick", editor="Finkel, Alain and Jantzen, Matthias", title="Deterministic regular languages", booktitle="STACS 92", year="1992", publisher="Springer Berlin Heidelberg", address="Berlin, Heidelberg", pages="173--184", abstract="The ISO standard for Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML) provides a syntactic meta-language for the definition of textual markup systems. In the standard the right hand sides of productions are called content models and they are based on regular expressions. The allowable regular expressions are those that are ``unambiguous'' as defined by the standard. Unfortunately, the standard's use of the term ``unambiguous'' does not correspond to the two well known notions, since not all regular languages are denoted by ``unambiguous'' expressions. Furthermore, the standard's definition of ``unambiguous'' is somewhat vague. Therefore, we provide a precise definition of ``unambiguous expressions'' and rename them deterministic regular expressions to avoid any confusion. A regular expression E is deterministic if the canonical $\epsilon$-free finite automaton Merecognizing L(E) is deterministic. A regular language is deterministic if there is a deterministic expression that denotes it. We give a Kleene-like theorem for deterministic regular languages and we characterize them in terms of the structural properties of the minimal deterministic automata recognizing them. The latter result enables us to decide if a given regular expression denotes a deterministic regular language and, if so, to construct an equivalent deterministic expression.", isbn="978-3-540-46775-5" }

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Thus far I have shown the soundness of our notions of nullability and first sets for the encoding of deterministic regular expresssions in Dependent Lambek Calculus.

I've been primarily stuck on the following proof for the soundness of the followlast sets in the case of concatenation of two nonnullable grammars.
Given g and h such that \mathsf {FLast}(g) and \mathsf {First}(h) are disjoint, and c \not \in \mathsf {FLast}(h), want to show that c is also not in \mathsf {FLast}(g \otimes h).
That is, assuming for all c, g \And {\mathopen {}\left (g \otimes c \otimes \top \right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \bot or h \And {\mathopen {}\left (c \otimes \top \right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \bot . Fix c such that h \And {\mathopen {}\left (h \otimes c \otimes \top \right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \bot , and then show g \otimes h \And {\mathopen {}\left (g \otimes h \otimes c \otimes \top \right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \bot .

This isn't super bad to do in the model, where you do some case analysis. In particular, the string that is parsed splits into some w , x : \mathrm {String} with g and h parses, respectively. Likewise, it splits into y , z : \mathrm {String} with a g parse of y and an h \otimes \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} \otimes \top parse of z. All in all, we have
w,x,y,z : \mathrm {String} , w \texttt { ++ } x = y \texttt { ++ } z with some parses g w, h x, g y, and (h \otimes \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} \otimes \top ) z. Then you split into cases checking whether w and y are the same string, if w is a (nontrivial) prefix of y, or if y is a prefix of w. Then each of the cases are straightforward enough but still tedious.

I've been weighing whether or not to do effectively the same proof but in the model by using the axiom g \cong \textstyle \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}. g \And \lceil w \rceil It feels as there should be a way to do this at a high level utilizing type-based reasoning, rather than manipulating individual strings.

The first set (\mathsf {First}(\cdot )) of a grammar A are all the characters that may appear at the beginning of a word in the language of A.
\mathsf {First}(A) = \{ c ~|~ \exists w . cw \in L(A) \}

The followlast set (\mathsf {FLast}(\cdot )) of a grammar A are all the characters that may follow a word in the language of A in a string that is in the language of A.
\mathsf {FLast}(A) = \{ c ~|~ \exists w , w_A . w_A \in L(A) \land w_Acw \in L(A) \}
A grammar A is nullable if the empty string belongs to the language of A.
